Australia's planned frigates will use Aegis combat systems, produced by Lockheed Martin, together with SAAB Australia technology, Turnbull said. Why now? Tensions in the region have soared in recent months as North Korea carried out a series of tests of its medium- and long-range ballistic missiles, some of which flew over Japan, as well as its sixth nuclear test on Sept. 3. Pyongyang, which ultimately wants to target the U.S. mainland with a nuclear-tipped ballistic missile, has openly said its missiles could strike Australia. Strike Australia! “Recent events in our region have proven that Australia's future frigates must be equipped to defend Australia from the threat of medium- and long-range missile attacks,” Turnbull said in a speech in Sydney. Work on the frigates is set to begin in 2020, with BAE Systems, Navantia and Fincantieri all battling for the A$35 billion ($27.39 billion) contract. Turnbull said the decision to award the missile defense system contract gives the three bidders enough time to build Aegis technology into their bids. title: Last-minute deal to kill North Carolina's bathroom law – but critics cry foul!
text: A dramatic late-night breakthrough! North Carolina Republican lawmakers said late on Wednesday they had struck a deal to repeal the state's notorious law barring transgender people from using restrooms in line with their gender identities. But is it really a repeal? The compromise, reached with Democratic Governor Roy Cooper and set to go before the legislature for a vote Thursday morning, would still ban local municipalities, schools and others from regulating bathroom access. It would also effectively block cities from offering their own job and restroom protections to vulnerable groups for nearly four years. “Compromise requires give and take from all sides, and we are pleased this proposal fully protects bathroom safety and privacy,” the state's top Republican lawmakers, Senate leader Phil Berger and House of Representatives Speaker Tim Moore, said in a statement released late Wednesday. The pair unveiled the deal at a hastily arranged news conference. And the timing is telling. The compromise with Cooper, a fierce opponent of the bathroom law, came just hours before the state was reportedly set to lose its ability to host any NCAA basketball championships. The college athletic association is one of a long list of organizations to sanction or boycott North Carolina since the law's passage last year. Cooper said earlier this week that the measure could end up costing the state a staggering nearly $4 billion. He backed the compromise. “It's not a perfect deal, but it repeals House Bill 2 and begins to repair our reputation.” Yet it remained unclear whether the deal would satisfy those who believe North Carolina was hostile to the rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people. In a fiery news conference before the deal was announced, several leading LGBT activists slammed its provisions, including the bar on municipalities regulating employment practices and “public accommodations”.

title: Ford Sollers begins serial production of cars with Era-Glonass system
text: The Ford Sollers joint venture has started installing Era-Glonass positioning systems across the entire line of Ford automobiles produced in Russia, the company's press service said on Oct. 27. "The whole model range of Ford vehicles for the Russian market will now have serially outfitted Ford emergency call system compatible with Era-Glonass emergency services calling system," the press service said. In the event of an accident, the vehicle's data and precise coordinates are identified automatically and transmitted to an operator of the Era-Glonass system and then to emergency services, either the 112 System or units of the Interior Ministry. All Ford cars for the Russian market will be equipped with the Era-Glonass system from January 1, 2017.

title: Merkel under fire: embattled chancellor races to Africa to stem the migrant tide
text: Angela Merkel is feeling the heat. The German Chancellor will focus on expanding business ties and trying to control migration from Africa at an EU-Africa summit in Abidjan this week, as pressure mounts at home for faster progress on both fronts. Merkel is taking a break from her drawn-out, more than month-long struggle to form a new government to attend the summit, eager to show that Germany can still act on the foreign policy front and to underline her commitment to Africa. She will team up with French President Emmanuel Macron at the summit to push education, investment in youth and economic development to stop refugees and economic migrants from attempting the treacherous journey across the Mediterranean. And treacherous it is. Libya is now the main departure point for mostly African migrants trying to reach Europe. Smugglers usually cram them into flimsy inflatable boats that often break down or sink. The chancellor told a conservative event on Saturday that she would press for expanded trade ties and investment, while urging African leaders in one-on-one talks to take back their citizens who had no right to stay in Europe. The stakes for her could not be higher. Merkel faces widespread criticism of her 2015 decision to let in over a million migrants, then mostly from the Middle East and Afghanistan. She is under pressure at home to prevent another migration crisis after bleeding support to the far right in the Sept. 24 election. Can she turn it around? Germany is likely to adopt an immigration law of some kind in the aftermath of election losses for mainstream parties.

title: Bizarre lawsuit: famous painter Peter Doig forced to prove he DIDN'T paint a canvas!
text: OK, Peter Doig may have tried LSD a few times when he was growing up in Canada during the 1970s. But he still knows, he said, when a painting is or isn't his. So when Mr. Doig, whose eerie, magical landscapes have made him one of the world's most popular artists, was sent a photograph of a canvas he said he didn't recognize, he disowned it. “I said, ‘Nice painting,’” he recalled in an interview. “‘Not by me.’” End of story? Far from it. The owner disagreed and sued him, setting up one of the strangest art authentication cases in recent history. The owner, a former corrections officer who said he knew Mr. Doig while working in a Canadian detention facility, insists the famous painter created the work as a youthful inmate there. His suit claims that Mr. Doig is either confused or lying and that his denials blew up a plan to sell the work for millions of dollars. Millions! But Mr. Doig, 57, has compelling evidence he was never near the facility, the Thunder Bay Correctional Center, about 15 hours north of Toronto. “This case is a scam, and I'm being forced to jump through hoops to prove my whereabouts over 40 years ago,” he said. And yet, to Mr. Doig's surprise and the astonishment of others in the art world, a federal judge in Chicago has set the case for trial next month at United States District Court for Northern Illinois. Art law experts say they can't recall anything like it, certainly not for a major artist like Mr. Doig. “To have to disprove that you created a work seems somehow wrong and not fair,” said Amy M. Adler, a professor at New York University Law School. And the stakes are high.

title: Under U.S. pressure, South Sudan's Kiir finally orders aid let through — Haley: 'We will be watching'
text: Finally! South Sudan's President Salva Kiir has ordered that humanitarian aid convoys be allowed to move freely, unhindered and unimpeded around the country — just two weeks after the United States declared it had lost trust in his government and threatened to pull support. The Nov. 9 order directs that all roadblocks be torn down, all levels of government must assist aid groups, and anyone who obstructs aid or imposes taxes on aid convoys shall be held accountable. The move came two weeks after U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley met with Kiir in Juba. She was the first member of President Donald Trump's cabinet to visit South Sudan, which plunged into civil war in late 2013, a mere two years after gaining independence from Sudan. "This is a good sign, but we must see actions - more than words from President Kiir," Haley said in a statement on Tuesday, referring to the Nov. 9 presidential order. "The true test will be whether humanitarian assistance is actually allowed to get to the South Sudanese people in a consistent way. We will be watching, and we will continue to encourage President Kiir to do the right thing," she said. Haley's office said Kiir had still not delivered on further commitments made during a 45-minute, one-on-one meeting with Haley in Juba. The war in South Sudan, sparked by a bitter feud between Kiir and his former deputy Riek Machar, has plunged parts of the world's youngest nation into famine. Some 4 million people have fled their homes — a third of the country's population. A staggering toll!

title: Federal appeals court strikes down North Carolina voter identification law
text: The United States 4th Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled against North Carolina Republicans over the state's voting law. In 2013, Republicans in North Carolina used their power to pass a law designed to keep them in power by suppressing the votes of minorities and young people through a requirement to bring voter identification. The law also cut early voting, ended same-day registration and heavily restricted pre-registration of young voters. It was the most restrictive anti-voting law in the country and has drawn large protests since its passage. Critics of the law challenged its constitutionality in court, and the district court ruled against them. The federal appeals court has now reversed the lower court's decision and criticized it. In holding that the legislature did not enact the challenged provisions with discriminatory intent, the court seems to have missed the forest in carefully surveying the many trees, Judge Diana Motz wrote in the decision. This failure of perspective led the court to ignore critical facts bearing on legislative intent, including the inextricable link between race and politics in North Carolina. Motz then criticized the Republican-dominated state legislature of North Carolina. The General Assembly enacted legislation that restricted voting and registration in five different ways, all of which disproportionately affected African Americans, she wrote, noting that the court had reviewed the record thoroughly before reaching its ruling. In response to claims that intentional racial discrimination animated its action, the State offered only meager justifications. Although the new provisions target African Americans with almost surgical precision, they constitute inapt remedies for the problems assertedly justifying them and, in fact, impose cures for problems that did not exist.

The court reviewed the record thoroughly before its ruling. In response to claims that intentional racial discrimination animated its action, the State offered only meager justifications. Although the new provisions target African Americans with almost surgical precision, they constitute inapt remedies for the problems assertedly justifying them and, in fact, impose cures for problems that did not exist.

title: Deadly 'superbug' horror at UCLA: 2 deaths possibly linked, 7 infected, 179 exposed!
text: A frightening outbreak at one of the country's top hospitals! UCLA reported Wednesday that nearly 180 patients were exposed to a potentially deadly "superbug" on contaminated medical instruments that infected seven patients and may have contributed to two deaths. A total of 179 patients at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center were exposed to antibiotic-resistant carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, or CRE, during endoscopic procedures between October and January, the university said in a statement. The bacteria may have been a "contributing factor" in the deaths of two patients, the university admitted. Those exposed are being sent free home-testing kits that the university will analyze. And it isn't just UCLA: similar outbreaks of CRE have been reported around the nation. They are notoriously difficult to treat because some varieties are resistant to most known antibiotics. How dangerous is it? By one estimate, CRE can contribute to death in up to half of seriously infected patients, according to the national Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The bacteria can cause infections of the bladder or lungs, leading to coughing, fever or chills. CRE infections have been reported in every state except Idaho, Alaska and Maine, according to the CDC. UCLA said infections may have been spread through specialized endoscopes used during the diagnosis and treatment of pancreatic and bile-duct problems. The instruments are inserted into the patients' throats. The outbreak was discovered only late last month during tests on a patient. Worse still, the two medical devices may have carried the bacteria even though they were sterilized according to the manufacturer's specifications, UCLA said. The devices have been removed, and decontamination procedures upgraded, the university said. "We notified all patients who had this type of procedure, and we were using seven different scopes. Only two of them were found to be infected. In an abundance of caution, we notified everybody," said Dale Tate, a University of California, Los Angeles spokeswoman.

title: Trump has been sued repeatedly over disability violations at his properties
text: Over the past 19 years, Donald Trump has been sued at least eight times for violations of the Americans with Disabilities Act at his various properties, and has sought to prolong these cases for as long as possible. In addition, a federal inspection at one of his properties found multiple ADA violations. Five of the cases ended in a settlement and two others were resolved in consent decrees that required Trump to make modifications to the properties to bring them into compliance with the ADA. One ended when both sides requested that the case be dismissed, and another was closed in a bankruptcy. Christine Da Silva, a Trump Hotels spokeswoman, said that Trump works very hard and spends a great deal of money to make sure his buildings are accessible to people with disabilities. It is the policy at all of our properties to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act. This handful of cases, many of which are over ten years old, are not representative of our organization's strong record of ADA compliance. However, that handful of cases is damaging and does not support Trump's claims. In a suit filed in 1997, James Conlon, who is paraplegic, sued Trump's Atlantic City Plaza Hotel alleging basic and serious deficiencies in accessibility. He stayed at the hotel, and although he was placed in a room that was supposedly accessible, the toilets and showers could not be used by someone in a wheelchair. The public restrooms were so inaccessible that he had to ask strangers for help to use them at all. A year later, Trump settled the case and agreed to renovate the accessible guest rooms and public restrooms, bringing them into compliance with the ADA.
